sampling_model.design: Complete randomization with a fixed treated count \(n_1\) and control count \(n_0=n-n_1\). The balanced case \(n_1=n_0=m\) and every unequal case \(n_1\neq n_0\) are analyzed separately.
sampling_model.units: The \(n=2m\) labeled units have fixed no-interference potential-outcome pairs summarized by \(R\in\mathcal R_0(n,K)\).
sampling_model.treatment: Exactly \(n_1\) units receive treatment and \(n_0\) receive control; balance means \(n_1=n_0=m\).
sampling_model.overlap: Every labeled assignment with the prescribed treated count has the same positive probability \(\binom{n}{n_1}^{-1}\), specialized to \(\binom{2m}{m}^{-1}\) under balance.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: There is no estimated nuisance. Exact claims are uniform over the finite set \(\mathcal R_0(n,K)\).

comparator_promise_table.comparator_claim: Proposition 3.1 characterizes invariant bijections for i.i.d. finite-support samples through equality of product probability masses.
Theorem 1 gives asymptotically conservative weak-null validity for a studentized Fisher randomization test on fixed finite populations.
Theorem 1 gives finite-sample level control for rank tests under an assumed finite-group invariance.
The paper constructs finite-sample exact confidence sets for the binary average treatment effect by prediction and randomization-test inversion.
Balanced binary exact confidence sets can be computed with \(O(n\log n)\) permutation tests, compared with \(O(n^2)\) generally.
Robustly studentized interacted OLS Fisher tests are finite-sample exact under the sharp null and asymptotically valid under the weak null.

body.tldr: Exact weak-null symmetry has an allocation-balance elbow and an exact sparse-separator phase diagram. Under balanced complete randomization, binary outcomes retain precisely the arm-transpose classes and have worst-case separator number zero. Alphabets with \(K\geq3\) retain only the opposing endpoint-corner pair; their worst-case separator number is two for \(m\in\{1,2\}\) and three for \(m\geq3\). Every unequal complete-randomization allocation has only singleton classes, identity maximal common group, and worst-case separator number two. Consequently conventional nonrandomized common-orbit ranks lie in \(\{1/2,1\}\) when balanced and are identically \(1\) when unequal. An explicit non-orbit exact p-value prevents any broader impossibility interpretation.

project_justification.gap: Weak-null randomization theory supplies asymptotic studentization or exact inversion over compatible schedules, while general permutation theory begins with a specified invariant group. It does not compute how the probability-equivalence partition of all fixed zero-average-effect schedules changes exactly at equal versus unequal arm allocation.
project_justification.niche: For a finite outcome alphabet, fixed potential-outcome schedules and complete randomization produce an exact multivariate-hypergeometric coefficient system. Computing its common stabilizer exposes allocation balance, rather than alphabet size alone, as the decisive symmetry boundary.
project_justification.fill: The paper classifies the balanced and unequal-arm equivalence partitions, derives their maximal common bijection groups, and certifies the complete finite-sample sparse-separator phase diagram. The balanced value is zero for \(K=2\), two for \(K\geq3\) with \(m\in\{1,2\}\), and three for \(K\geq3\) with \(m\geq3\); every unequal allocation has value two. It then derives the corresponding conventional orbit-rank granularity while retaining a constructive non-orbit exact counterexample to any general impossibility claim.

body.related_work: \cite{WuDing2021} frames the weak-null obstacle through missing potential outcomes and obtains asymptotic control by studentization. \cite{HemerikGoeman2018} supplies orbit-counting validity once a finite invariant group is given; here the group is computed from the full composite causal null. \cite{DutzZhang2026} concerns invariant bijections for i.i.d. finite-support product laws. The present paper instead conditions on a fixed potential-outcome schedule and studies assignment-induced multivariate-hypergeometric laws. Neither model class is a subclass of the other for purposes of these results, and no converse, invariance classification, or separator bound is transferred between them. \cite{RigdonHudgens2015} and \cite{LiDing2016} obtain exact binary average-effect confidence sets through compatible-table reasoning rather than a common group, while \cite{AronowChangLopatto2025} gives a balanced computational acceleration for that inversion problem. \cite{ChungRomano2013} studies unequal group proportions through asymptotic multinomial--hypergeometric coupling; the unequal-allocation result here is an exact fixed-schedule coefficient classification. \cite{ZhaoDing2021} supplies the robustly studentized weak-null workflow motivating the applied audit, but its weak-null guarantee is asymptotic rather than the common-invariance and sparse-separator statements studied here.
body.technical_internal_limitation: The cubic separator and the lower bound against every legal schedule with at most two heterogeneous units are needed only when \(K\geq3\) and \(m\geq3\). For \(m\in\{1,2\}\), the exceptional endpoint equation would require distinct positive integers summing to \(m\), so explicit two-unit switches suffice; binary inequivalent pairs are already separated by a diagonal table. The \(K=3,n=6\) enumeration, which gives cubic counts \(1\) and \(0\) and checks all \(103\) legal tables with \(q(R)\leq2\), remains only a diagnostic stress test. Separator complexity counts heterogeneous units, not enumeration time or statistical power. The exact group result also does not justify replacing the HC2 or robust-\(t\) weak-null workflow, whose guarantee and objective are different.
body.honest_scope: The results concern fixed no-interference schedules, complete randomization with positive fixed arm sizes, histogram-measurable common bijections, and equally spaced finite alphabets. They cover both balanced and unequal allocations: the balanced partition has the stated transpose or endpoint-corner classes, whereas every unequal partition is singleton. The balanced worst-case separator number is zero for binary outcomes, two for nonbinary outcomes with \(m\in\{1,2\}\), and three for nonbinary outcomes with \(m\geq3\); the unequal worst-case value is two over its stated admissible range. The orbit-rank conclusion applies only to conventional nonrandomized ranks generated by a schedule-universal group. It does not classify every exact weak-null test, validate a particular sharp-null permutation statistic, or cover covariate-adaptive, stratified, or clustered designs.
